cl_inh_sudden_death.q: Can sniffing solvents cause sudden death?
cl_inh_sudden_death.short: Sudden deaths after sniffing solvents and sprays were reported in one old survey.
cl_inh_sudden_death.but: It counted deaths, without measuring risk among everyone who used these products.
how: A 1969 US survey described 110 deaths among young people aged 11 to 23, mostly involving sprays or a cleaning solvent. The report did not list poppers.
In several witnessed deaths, the person suddenly ran or panicked before collapsing. Where autopsies were described, they found no other cause.
The author proposed an effect on the heart's rhythm. No heart trace was recorded.
Families or friends hid the sniffing in 8 deaths, so some other deaths may have been missed.

cl_mdma_preloading_practices.q: What do people do before and after ecstasy to lower harm?
cl_mdma_preloading_practices.short: People reported drinking water, taking breaks and using supplements; benefits were not tested.
cl_mdma_preloading_practices.but: One self-selected group of 116 adults in Australia in 2004.
how: A 2004 Australian survey asked 116 people who had used ecstasy about their habits. They chose to answer, so the figures do not represent everyone who uses ecstasy.
Almost all reported drinking water to avoid side effects; most reported limiting how much they used or taking breaks.
About 4 in 10 reported taking vitamins or other products before ecstasy, and about half afterwards. Reasons included easing the comedown and seeking more pleasure.
About 4 in 10 had ever tested their pills. This survey did not measure whether any of these practices worked.

cl_mdma_hyponatremia.short: Some young people were treated for low blood salt (sodium) after taking MDMA.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia.but: These are reports of people who became ill, so they cannot show how often it happens.
how: In 17 people aged 15 to 26 reported to a UK poisons service, at least 10 had drunk a lot of fluid. Two died; each had taken one tablet, had drunk a lot of water, and drank or was given more after feeling ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level, and 4 of those 73 died.
The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water, which waters down the salt in the blood; the UK authors say how it does this is not yet known.
No paper compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, so none can show whether taking more makes it more likely.

cl_mdma_hyponatremia_risk.short: Women with MDMA illness more often had low blood salt than men did.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia_risk.but: These are people who became ill and had a blood test, not everyone who takes MDMA.
how: Of 105 women with a blood salt test, 55 (52 in 100) had a low level; of 83 men, 18 (22 in 100) did.
Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma than women without one; in men the numbers were too small to tell.
A UK group (10 of 17 were women) and a review of published cases (more than 85 in 100 were female) point the same way, but the review's cases overlap with the California ones.

A review describes one controlled study in 8 women and 8 men given the same MDMA amount. A hormone marker rose only in the women; the review does not identify the comparison behind its other hormone and sodium results. This does not establish why women were more common in the reported cases.

cl_coc_heat.q: Are cocaine deaths more common in hot weather, and why?
cl_coc_heat.short: In 1990s New York, hot days had a third more cocaine overdose deaths.
cl_coc_heat.but: The study compared days, not people, and did not allow for season.
how: In New York City in 1993 to 1995, there were 2.34 cocaine overdose deaths a day on hot days and 1.76 on other days.

Deaths in the opiate group, where cocaine was absent or present only in amounts judged clinically insignificant, did not clearly rise. The study could not show that the rise happened only with cocaine.

In a lab, 7 healthy people who had never used cocaine were warmed in a heated suit after one small dose. They began to sweat later, warmed up more and felt less hot than after a numbing drug used for comparison.
The lab study used one small dose in people at rest, so it may not match real use in hot weather.
